text.preview:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

articles.title: Solar Philippines completes Southeast Asia’s largest solar-battery micro-grid in Mindoro
articles.description: Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

text.preview:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

The micro-grid was built in Paluan, Occidental Mindoro.

With 2 megawatts (MW) of solar panels, 2 megawatt hours (MWh) of batteries, and 2 MW of diesel backup, the micro-grid “is designed to supply reliable power 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at 50 percent less than the full cost of the local electric coop,” Solar Philippines noted in an emailed statement.

The project uses panels from the Solar Philippines Factory, and is also the first micro-grid in Asia to feature Powerpacks from Tesla, a leading manufacturer of batteries and electric vehicles.

The project marks the launch of “Solar Para Sa Bayan” initiative by Solar Philippines founder Leandro Leviste to bring cheaper, more reliable power to areas poorly served by utilities, in support of the Duterte administration’s aim of ending energy poverty by 2022.

Paluan first received four hours of daily service in 1978 from the Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO), which later waived its franchise given the difficulties in serving the town, Mayor Carl Pangilinan said in his welcome remarks.
In 2014, National Power Corporation (NPC) resumed electricity service at an average of 16 hours a day but with outages sometimes lasting several days.

Pangilinan noted that since Solar Philippines began operations in December 2017, Palueños enjoyed their first ever Christmas without brownouts. He said students can study at night and use computers in school, families can use electric fans amid the summer heat, sari-sari stores can sell refrigerated drinks, and an ice plant is now being planned to support local fishermen.

Paluan used to consume subsidies of over P30 million a year under the NPC. With solar power now available, the town can consume electricity at 50 percent lower than the electricity from NPC.

text.preview:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

With 2 megawatts (MW) of solar panels, 2 megawatt hours (MWh) of batteries, and 2 MW of diesel backup, the micro-grid “is designed to supply reliable power 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at 50 percent less than the full cost of the local electric coop,” Solar Philippines noted in an emailed statement.

article.title: Solar Philippines completes Southeast Asia’s largest solar-battery micro-grid in Mindoro
article.description: Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

text.preview:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

The micro-grid was built in Paluan, Occidental Mindoro.

With 2 megawatts (MW) of solar panels, 2 megawatt hours (MWh) of batteries, and 2 MW of diesel backup, the micro-grid “is designed to supply reliable power 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at 50 percent less than the full cost of the local electric coop,” Solar Philippines noted in an emailed statement.

The project uses panels from the Solar Philippines Factory, and is also the first micro-grid in Asia to feature Powerpacks from Tesla, a leading manufacturer of batteries and electric vehicles.

The project marks the launch of “Solar Para Sa Bayan” initiative by Solar Philippines founder Leandro Leviste to bring cheaper, more reliable power to areas poorly served by utilities, in support of the Duterte administration’s aim of ending energy poverty by 2022.

Paluan first received four hours of daily service in 1978 from the Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO), which later waived its franchise given the difficulties in serving the town, Mayor Carl Pangilinan said in his welcome remarks.
In 2014, National Power Corporation (NPC) resumed electricity service at an average of 16 hours a day but with outages sometimes lasting several days.

Pangilinan noted that since Solar Philippines began operations in December 2017, Palueños enjoyed their first ever Christmas without brownouts. He said students can study at night and use computers in school, families can use electric fans amid the summer heat, sari-sari stores can sell refrigerated drinks, and an ice plant is now being planned to support local fishermen.

Paluan used to consume subsidies of over P30 million a year under the NPC. With solar power now available, the town can consume electricity at 50 percent lower than the electricity from NPC.

article.title: ICSC finds over 1,800MW potential solar rooftop capacity in the PH, as it launches SPECTRUM solar mapping tool
article.description: These numbers mean the Philippines could actually avoid an estimated grid emissions of about 1.8MTCOe (million tons of CO2 equivalent), explained ICSC's Chief Data Scientist Jephraim Manansala to GMA News Online.

text.preview:
The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC) officially launched SPECTRUM (Solar Power Estimation of Capacities and Tracking Using Machine Learning), a groundbreaking online platform designed to map, monitor, and accelerate the growth of rooftop solar energy systems across the Philippines.

At the launch event Tuesday, ICSC Chief Data Scientist Jephraim Manansala presented SPECTRUM’s core features, highlighting its capacity to track existing rooftop solar installations nationwide using machine learning.

The platform is intended to support local governments, utilities, solar developers, and communities in planning and implementing solar energy programs.

“SPECTRUM is more than just a mapping tool, although it is a fancy mapping tool,” said ICSC Executive Director Angelo Kairos Dela Cruz. “It is a bold leap toward a future where innovation meets inclusion."

Currently, SPECTRUM maps rooftop solar capacities in 174 cities and municipalities, with an initial focus on high-density urban areas where rooftop solar penetration is highest. Given this coverage, the tool has already helped detect 1,309.64 megawatts (MW) of potential solar rooftop capacity in Luzon, 472.48MW capacity in Visayas, and 61.08MW capacity in Mindanao –– amounting to 1,846.08MW potential solar capacity nationwide.

Of the total 1,846.08MW, 1,398.25MW are utility scale, 202.03MW are commercial, and 245.8MW are residential installations.

article.title: Smileys, Solar Boys off to winning start in PSA Cup
article.description: The Say Chiz Smileys had the last laugh after surviving a close one against the Smart Sports Scribes while the Capital1 Solar Boys delivered a wire-to-wire victory over the Strong Group Athletics Press Row Bros in the opening of the 2024 Philippine Sportswriters Association Cup at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium on Tuesday.
article.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Say Chiz Smileys had the last laugh after surviving a close one against the Smart Sports Scribes while the Capital1 Solar Boys delivered a wire-to-wire victory over the Strong Group Athletics Press Row Bros in the opening of the 2024 Philippine Sportswriters Association (PSA) Cup at the Ninoy Aquino Stadium on Tuesday. An eventual game-winning floater from Jeric Lopez with 39 seconds left, a big offensive rebound by Aivan Episcope, and crucial stops in the last 8.4 seconds helped the Smileys of Philippine Daily Inquirer’s Francis Ochoa escape the Smart-backed side of Spin.PH’s Dodo Catacutan, 66-64, in the tournament which is one of the projects of PSA resident Nelson Beltran of The Philippine STAR. In the first game, Christian Jacinto and birthday boy Aldo Aviñante were all business for Capital1 of Manila Bulletin’s Ramon Bonilla, leading the squad to an 86-74 victory against SGA. The tournament inaugurals were graced by Philippine Sports Commission chairman Richard Bachmann and ACES chief Dr. Ian Laurel. Jonas Terrado of the Inquirer finished with game-highs 21 points and 14 rebounds, along with four steals, two assists, and a block. Lopez followed with 16 points, three rebounds, and four assists while Cedelf Tupas added 15 points, four assists, and four steals. AJ Bolando topscored for Smart Sports with 19 points, but was limited to two points in the fourth quarter. article.title: Solar Philippines completes Southeast Asia’s largest solar-battery micro-grid in Mindoro
article.description: Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

text.preview:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

The micro-grid was built in Paluan, Occidental Mindoro.

With 2 megawatts (MW) of solar panels, 2 megawatt hours (MWh) of batteries, and 2 MW of diesel backup, the micro-grid “is designed to supply reliable power 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at 50 percent less than the full cost of the local electric coop,” Solar Philippines noted in an emailed statement.

The project uses panels from the Solar Philippines Factory, and is also the first micro-grid in Asia to feature Powerpacks from Tesla, a leading manufacturer of batteries and electric vehicles.

The project marks the launch of “Solar Para Sa Bayan” initiative by Solar Philippines founder Leandro Leviste to bring cheaper, more reliable power to areas poorly served by utilities, in support of the Duterte administration’s aim of ending energy poverty by 2022.

Paluan first received four hours of daily service in 1978 from the Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO), which later waived its franchise given the difficulties in serving the town, Mayor Carl Pangilinan said in his welcome remarks.
In 2014, National Power Corporation (NPC) resumed electricity service at an average of 16 hours a day but with outages sometimes lasting several days.

Pangilinan noted that since Solar Philippines began operations in December 2017, Palueños enjoyed their first ever Christmas without brownouts. He said students can study at night and use computers in school, families can use electric fans amid the summer heat, sari-sari stores can sell refrigerated drinks, and an ice plant is now being planned to support local fishermen.

Paluan used to consume subsidies of over P30 million a year under the NPC. With solar power now available, the town can consume electricity at 50 percent lower than the electricity from NPC.

He identified four officials of the Bulacan First District Engineering Office (DEO): former district engineer Henry Alcantara, former assistant district engineer Brice Ericson Hernandez, former construction section chief Jaypee Mendoza, and Project Engineer Arjay Domasig. He also named one contractor: Edrick San Diego. On September 11, corruption charges were filed before the Office of the Ombudsman against officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), which include the four DPWH officials named by Lacson. Alcantara, Hernandez, and Mendoza were all dismissed from service as of this writing. Flood control scandal, contractors at the core President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. launched on August 11 the ‘Sumbong sa Pangulo’ website, setting off the Philippine flood control scandal , which has drawn attention nationwide for over a month now. This controversy involves public officials and private contractors who allegedly schemed to bag billions of government money through substandard and ‘ghost’ flood mitigation projects. Bulacan tops flood control projects Bulacan leads in terms of both the highest cumulative cost and number of flood control projects among provinces, besides Metro Manila . Among flood projects in Luzon , those implemented in Bulacan were thrust into the spotlight when authorities uncovered some anomalous projects in the area. Several of Bulacan’s 668 flood control projects, totaling P43.8 billion, were found by Marcos, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon, and the Commission on Audit as either substandard, incomplete, non-existent, or overpriced. These anomalous flood control projects in Bulacan include: Project Contractor Amount Issues Flagged Flood control structure in Bgys. Buguion, Sergio Bayan, Balite, San Marcos, Palimbang, in Calumpit St. Timothy Construction Company P39 million Government overpaid by P3 million without any documentation and is substandard Riverwall project in Bgy. Piel in Baliuag SYMS Construction Trading P55 million No construction seen onsite Flood mitigation structures in Bgy. Sta. Lucia in Calumpit Wawao Builders P74 million Declared as almost finished but is not the case on site; already deteriorating Flood mitigation structure in Bgy. Frances in Calumpit Wawao Builders P77.2 million Still incomplete but already listed as fully finished River protection structure in Bgy. Bulusan in Calumpit St. Timothy Construction Company P96.4 million Overpriced with a P38.5 million discrepancy Flood control structure in Bgy. Sipat in Plaridel Wawao Builders P96.5 million Declared as fully completed but construction was still ongoing on site on September 4, 2025 Except for San Diego, whom Lacson identified as a contractor, the alleged BGC Boys – Alcantara, Hernandez, Mendoza, and Domasig – worked at Bulacan First DEO that implemented the said anomalous projects. Henry Alcantara’s rise through the ranks In under three weeks, Alcantara went from relieved to dismissed to facing graft charges over anomalies in flood control projects in Bulacan. On August 22, Alcantara was reported as one of the 10 DPWH officials placed on floating status and was relieved from his position as assistant regional director of DPWH Region IV-A. On September 4, he was dismissed from service, then a week later, on September 11, he was among 20 district engineers facing graft complaints. During the first House hearing on anomalous flood control projects, Alcantara said he graduated with an engineering degree from the University of Santo Tomas. He also said he started as a job order employee at the DPWH in 1994 and revealed that he rose through the ranks, going from Laborer 1 to Laborer 2 to Engineer 1, every six months. In 2019, he was designated as the officer-in-charge (OIC) district engineer of Bulacan’s First DEO by then DPWH chief and now Senator Mark Villar. Just recently, in June 2025, Alcantara said he was promoted to OIC assistant regional director of DPWH Region IV-A. His previous position in Bulacan was taken over by his then-assistant district engineer, Brice Hernandez. During the same House hearing, Alcantara admitted to certifying the completion of alleged ghost projects without conducting site inspections, stating that he relied on his team and the documents they submitted. His team at the time included the other three persons Lacson named – Hernandez, Mendoza, and Domasig – and accountant Juanito Mendoza. He was linked to the P55 million riverwall project of SYMS Construction Trading in Baliuag that was discovered by Marcos as having no visible work. He also approved alleged ghost projects of St. Timothy Construction Company, owned by Cezarah Rowena ‘Sarah’ Discaya, and Wawao Builders. In the second House hearing, Alcantara refused to sign waivers that would allow access to his bank and phone records. However, he said he is willing to disclose his Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth submitted when he was a district engineer. In the same hearing, Alcantara was also dubbed by Hernandez as their ‘chief implementor’ who allegedly talks to politicians about their schemes. According to Hernandez, Alcantara gets a three percent kickback on all the projects under their office. Alcantara denied such claims. In the first House hearing, Alcantara admitted to gambling in casinos at least two to three times a month. He said he has been gambling since mid-2023 despite knowing that government officials are prohibited from doing so. When asked how much money he loses in casinos every month, Alcantara said ‘P100,000.’ According to Lacson, Alcantara lost at least P36.7 million in casinos both under his real name and his alias ‘Joseph Castro Villegas.’ He described Alcantara and Hernandez as ‘having the same love for money.’ Brice Ericson Hernandez and his luxury cars Hernandez graduated from De La Salle University and passed the civil engineering licensure exam in 2008. In the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee hearing on flood control projects, Hernandez was flagged for his luxury car collection despite only earning P70,000 monthly as a district engineer, a position he assumed just three months ago. Hernandez replaced Alcantara as the district engineer of Bulacan First DEO in June 2025. Lacson said Hernandez also had gambling habits and used ‘Marvin Santos De Guzman’ as an alias at casinos. He allegedly lost P435 million to gambling. Hernandez was cited in contempt by the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee after supposedly lying about his casino visits and is currently in custody of Pasay City Jail . In the second House hearing, Hernandez linked Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Joel Villanueva to Alcantara and Mendoza in the corruption scheme involving flood control projects. Hernandez said he was in contact with Sally Santos, owner of SYMS Construction Trading, who admitted to delivering millions of cash to his office. Unlike Alcantara, Hernandez said he is willing to sign waivers that would allow authorities to probe his bank and phone records. Jaypee Mendoza from Malolos Hailing from Malolos City, Mendoza succeeded Hernandez as the assistant district engineer of the Bulacan First DEO in June 2025. Prior to this, he was the construction section chief. According to Lacson, Mendoza lost around P418 million to gambling in casinos under the name of 'Peejay Castro Asunción.’ In the second House hearing, Hernandez revealed Mendoza as the one who took the photos of Alcantara’s alleged Viber conversation with Senator Villanueva in October 2023. Alcantara also named him as among those who would initially sign documents before they reach Alcantara’s approval. Later in the hearing, Mendoza asked that he and his family be immediately provided with security after receiving threats while the plenary was ongoing. According to him, on September 1, a day before he came to the committee hearing as a resource person, Mendoza received a Viber message from an account named ‘hitman.’ He did not describe further what the message was. On the day of the hearing, Mendoza said that the same ‘hitman’ contact was trying to call him right before he spoke. Arjay Domasig, the youngest engineer Domasig is the youngest DPWH engineer of the BGC Boys, having gotten his license in May 2016. He graduated from Bulacan State University and is now an Engineer II of Bulacan First DEO. Lacson said Domasig allegedly lost P16.9 million to gambling while he won P7.4 million at Newport World Resorts in a span of seven months. Together with Hernandez and Mendoza, he lost P1.75 million in one gaming activity at Okada Manila. Lacson said Domasig was presenting himself as a contractor from ‘SYMS Trading Corporation’ using the alias ‘Sandro Bernardo Park.’ Lacson listed three projects of the SYMS Construction Trading that were alleged to have been completed with questionable speed on paper to obtain progress billing payments. One project in Bulakan and another in Calumpit were allegedly nonexistent. Domasig was also the project engineer of the previously mentioned riverwall project in Baliuag that was contracted to SYMS Construction Trading. In the second House hearing, Domasig claimed Mendoza forced him to sign the said project’s work accomplishments. Mendoza was at the time the construction section chief and reported to Hernandez and Alcantara. Edrick San Diego, the lab tech There is little information on San Diego, except for the details Lacson revealed. Lacson identified San Diego as a contractor and called him the ‘lab tech’ of the ‘BGC Boys.’ Lacson alleged that San Diego lost P42.4 million to gambling and won P11.8 million at Newport World Resorts alone from August 31, 2023 to April 4, 2024.

output.title: Solar Philippines completes Southeast Asia’s largest solar-battery micro-grid in Mindoro
output.description: Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.
output.text:
Solar Philippines has completed the largest solar-battery micro-grid in Southeast Asia, the company said on Monday.

The micro-grid was built in Paluan, Occidental Mindoro.

With 2 megawatts (MW) of solar panels, 2 megawatt hours (MWh) of batteries, and 2 MW of diesel backup, the micro-grid “is designed to supply reliable power 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at 50 percent less than the full cost of the local electric coop,” Solar Philippines noted in an emailed statement.

The project uses panels from the Solar Philippines Factory, and is also the first micro-grid in Asia to feature Powerpacks from Tesla, a leading manufacturer of batteries and electric vehicles.

The project marks the launch of “Solar Para Sa Bayan” initiative by Solar Philippines founder Leandro Leviste to bring cheaper, more reliable power to areas poorly served by utilities, in support of the Duterte administration’s aim of ending energy poverty by 2022.

Paluan first received four hours of daily service in 1978 from the Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO), which later waived its franchise given the difficulties in serving the town, Mayor Carl Pangilinan said in his welcome remarks.
In 2014, National Power Corporation (NPC) resumed electricity service at an average of 16 hours a day but with outages sometimes lasting several days.

Pangilinan noted that since Solar Philippines began operations in December 2017, Palueños enjoyed their first ever Christmas without brownouts. He said students can study at night and use computers in school, families can use electric fans amid the summer heat, sari-sari stores can sell refrigerated drinks, and an ice plant is now being planned to support local fishermen.

Paluan used to consume subsidies of over P30 million a year under the NPC. With solar power now available, the town can consume electricity at 50 percent lower than the electricity from NPC.

“We see ourselves as partners in developing Paluan into a first-class municipality in the coming years. While other companies seek to charge the highest rates possible, we believe that offering quality service at the lowest cost is win-win, helping the areas we serve and growing the market over the long-term,” Leviste said. —VDS, GMA News

output.title: Corruption and ghost projects are the 'true horror stories': solon | ABS-CBN News
output.description: Corruption and “ghost projects” are the “true horror stories” this Halloween according to Gabriela Party List Representative Sarah Elago.
output.text: Workers shovel sand from a flooded school property to higher ground at Linagit Primary School in Barangay Meyto, Calumpit, Bulacan, on September 10, 2025. Jonathan Cellona, ABS-CBN News/File MANILA -- Corruption and “ghost projects” are the “true horror stories” this Halloween, according to Gabriela Party List Representative Sarah Elago. “Ang tunay na horror story sa ating bansa ngayon ay ang mga ghost projects at matinding korupsyon… Punong-puno ng trick or treat ang gobyerno ngayon. Trick o panlilinlang, dahil sa matinding mga pangungurakot sa mamamayang Pilipino, at mga treats naman para sa mga sariling interes at mga kontraktor,” Elago said. “Panawagan namin, ang tanging paraan para mapatay ang mga halimaw ng korupsyon ay ang sama-samang pagkilos ng taong bayan,” she added. ACT Teachers Party List Representative Antonio Tinio, for his part, said that this Halloween, those who should be “scared” are goverment officials involved in corruption because there will be no let up in the public’s call for accountability and justice. “Ngayong Halloween at Undas tayo, dapat na kilabutan ang mga kurakot dahil hindi sila tatantanan ng taong bayan sa panawagan para sa pagpapanagot at hustisya,” he said. Akbayan Party List Representative Percival Cendaña shares this sentiment. “’Yung pinakamatindi multo ay ‘yung multo na ninanakawan tayo, ‘yung multo ng corruption… Dapat tandaan natin na ‘yung mga multo na ito, sila dapat ang matakot sa atin kasi tumitindi na talaga ang galit ng taumbayan. Hindi lamang dito sa Metro Manila, kundi sa buong bansa. Kaya ‘yung mga halimaw ng korupsyon, maghintay sila kasi hindi magiging happy ang Halloween nila,” he said. READ: Some flood control projects were harmful, will have to be demolished -- Dizon 'INIP IS REAL' Cendaña and Tinio believe the public’s growing impatience for accountability on alleged anomalous flood control projects are justified. Tinio also expressed alarm and dismay that the Independent Commission for Infrastructure has yet to file cases against any legislators allegedly involved in the anomalies. “Napakarami nang lumabas na testimonya from resource persons directly involved para sabihin na hindi pa madidiinan ‘yung mga senators, members of Congress, and so on. So I think justified ‘yung pagkainip at frustration ng ating mga kababayan sa naipapakita ng ICI so far” he said. “Inip is real… Napakatagal na nung panahon mula nang sinabi ng Pangulo, noong SONA, hanggang sa ngayon, wala pa rin talagang napapanagot dito sa pagnanakaw sa kaban ng bayan. So while they're saying that they're doing it according to their own pace. Tandaan natin, kapag mas nagtatagal, mas pabor ito doon sa mga akusado… Kaya, sa lalong madaling panahon, they have to show ano ‘yung fruits ng kanilang naging trabaho,” Cendaña added. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro had urged the public to be more patient with the system, saying that the government was doing what it could to file cases against involved parties amid the deluge of data and cases linked to questionable anti-flood programs. READ: DENR flags 'poorly situated projects' affecting flow of rivers NO GIFT POLICY On whether Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo’s no gift policy across all local government offices should be replicated nationwide, Gabriela Party List Representative Sarah Elago said “Why not?” Tinio, for his part, noted that it is already part of existing anti-corruption measures in the government, but should be enforced strictly. In a Facebook post, Senator Robin Padilla commented, “Ganito rin si VP Inday Sara”. But Cendaña countered and pointed out that Robredo is “far” from Vice President Duterte. “Malayo si VP Leni kay VP Sara, kasi si VP Leni walang confidential funds na hanggang ngayon hindi pa napapaliwanag,” Cendaña said.

output.title: ICSC finds over 1,800MW potential solar rooftop capacity in the PH, as it launches SPECTRUM solar mapping tool
output.description: These numbers mean the Philippines could actually avoid an estimated grid emissions of about 1.8MTCOe (million tons of CO2 equivalent), explained ICSC's Chief Data Scientist Jephraim Manansala to GMA News Online.
output.text:
The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC) officially launched SPECTRUM (Solar Power Estimation of Capacities and Tracking Using Machine Learning), a groundbreaking online platform designed to map, monitor, and accelerate the growth of rooftop solar energy systems across the Philippines.

At the launch event Tuesday, ICSC Chief Data Scientist Jephraim Manansala presented SPECTRUM’s core features, highlighting its capacity to track existing rooftop solar installations nationwide using machine learning.

The platform is intended to support local governments, utilities, solar developers, and communities in planning and implementing solar energy programs.

“SPECTRUM is more than just a mapping tool, although it is a fancy mapping tool,” said ICSC Executive Director Angelo Kairos Dela Cruz. “It is a bold leap toward a future where innovation meets inclusion."

Currently, SPECTRUM maps rooftop solar capacities in 174 cities and municipalities, with an initial focus on high-density urban areas where rooftop solar penetration is highest. Given this coverage, the tool has already helped detect 1,309.64 megawatts (MW) of potential solar rooftop capacity in Luzon, 472.48MW capacity in Visayas, and 61.08MW capacity in Mindanao –– amounting to 1,846.08MW potential solar capacity nationwide.

Of the total 1,846.08MW, 1,398.25MW are utility scale, 202.03MW are commercial, and 245.8MW are residential installations.

These spectacular numbers mean the Philippines could actually avoid an estimated grid emissions of about 1.8MTCOe (million tons of CO2 equivalent), explained ICSC's Chief Data Scientist Jephraim Manansala to GMA News Online.

"However, note that this just for the selected areas in the country and still does not account for other areas," he advised.

Manansala came up with the estimated carbon avoidance by "assuming a 16% capacity factor for solar and using the Department of Energy's Operating Margin Emission Factors (2019-2021) of Luzon and Visayas at 0.6936 tCO2/MWh and Mindanao at 0.8522 tCO2/MWh.

"These values mean that for every 1MWh of solar electricity added, you're avoiding around 0.69-0.85 tons of Co2, depending on the region," Manansala continued.

Climate change is caused by the burning of fossil fuels, which then produces greenhouse gas emissions and traps the sun's heat in the atmosphere.

Avoiding carbon is important in the fight against climate change, which is why transitioning away from fossil fuels and into clean energy is important.

This is especially important for the Philippines, which is already experiencing the effects of climate change. Last year, the country experienced four simultaneous typhoons, which the World Weather Attribution said was made 70% more likely as a result of climate change.

According to the German Watch's Climate Risk Index 2025, the Philippines is the 10th most affected country by extreme weather events in the last 30 years, making the transition to clean energy urgent.

SPECTRUM was launched on Tuesday morning at Novotel Manila in Araneta City, Cubao, where key stakeholders from the government, diplomatic corps, energy sector, and civil society were present.

In attendance were Department of Energy (DOE) Undersecretary Felix William Fuentebella and Assistant Secretary Mylene Capongcol, along with Elizabeth Thompson, Barbados Ambassador for Climate Change, Small Island Developing States (SIDS), and the Law of the Sea. Climate Vulnerable Forum–V20 Secretary-General and former Maldives President Mohamed Nasheed also delivered a keynote address, underscoring the regional and global significance of scaling up clean energy.

A panel discussion followed, featuring representatives from the DOE, Energy Regulatory Commission, Meralco, and Quezon City local government, who discussed policy implications, opportunities, and integration with existing energy systems.

The launch was capped off by a hands-on workshop, giving members of the academe, civil society, and other energy advocates the opportunity to interact with the tool and offer feedback on its usability and future development.

From the current 175 174 cities and municipalities, ICSC aims to expand SPECTRUM's coverage to up to 400 cities and municipalities within the coming month.

Accessible for free online, SPECTRUM is expected to play a key role in promoting net metering, identifying solar-ready zones, and supporting the Philippines’ broader renewable energy transition. — With reports from Sherylin Untalan/LA GMA Integrated News

output.title: BirdTalk 2026: PH needs not only good governance but also good economics
output.description: Ibon’s Rosario Guzman: The nation’s structure is collapsing because of political instability and a fragile economy due to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s ‘blunders.’ The first was adopting an anti-corruption stance in announcing the anomalous flood control projects while remaining silent on the pork barrel issue.
output.text: Liana Garcellano has been crisscrossing the worlds of writing and teaching in her professional career. After graduation from UP Diliman, she ... Liana Garcellano has been crisscrossing the worlds of writing and teaching in her professional career. After graduation from UP Diliman, she ... Year 2026 is just on its second month, yet despondency appears to hang over the country. Filipinos struggling to make ends meet have been confronting seven straight weeks of increases in fuel prices. The flood control corruption scandal has yet to be resolved. Elsewhere, in the West Philippine Sea, the Coast Guard struggles to uphold our sovereign rights, and the facts behind our Kalayaan Island Group need to be explained to the public at large, including certain senators. The prospects seem even grimmer after hearing the situationer of the Ibon Foundation’s Sonny Africa and Rosario Guzman at the 2026 Ibon BirdTalk held on Jan. 23 at the UP Statistics Auditorium. Titled “From Frustration to Action,” the first of the bi-annual talks had Africa and Guzman, Ibon executive director and research head, respectively, explaining how structural weaknesses have led to a bleak economy and a political crisis. “We don’t just want good governance…we want good economics,” Africa said. “The government isn’t good at achieving targets. Since 2016, it has failed to meet its growth targets for the coming year 90 percent of the time.” His data analysis shows that economic growth fell even three years before the pandemic, with the growth for 2025 plunging to a low 5.7 percent. The high growth period of 2004-2016 — 6.6 percent in 2004 and 7.1 percent in 2016 — are long gone, he said, adding: “The economy was growing fast but the slowdown started in 2017 and is continuing up to now, which is contrary to the Marcos Jr. government’s claim of rapid growth.” Africa’s slide presentation titled “Philippine economy after three years of Marcos Jr.” juxtaposed his findings on the growing number of poor and hungry Filipinos vis-á-vis the burgeoning wealth of a few. Figures for the former showed self-rated poor families reaching 14.3 million; involuntary hungry families totaling 5.7 million; and borderline poor and vulnerable families rising to 17.7 million. Conversely, the three richest Filipinos became even richer. According to Africa, Enrique Razon’s wealth increased 115 percent or an additional ₱351 billion; Ramon Ang’s wealth rose by 62 percent or an additional ₱83 billion; and Manny Villar’s wealth grew by 48 percent or an additional ₱203 billion. Africa said household spending was the biggest driver for economic growth because of the “additional 10 million [people] spending.” But household spending weakened after 2017, when wage increase stagnated, remittances from overseas dropped, and foreign direct investment inflows fell. Services filled the gap but they were not of high quality and could not compensate for the lost jobs in the agriculture and manufacturing sectors, he said. He argued that external sources should not be driving growth, and pointed out that “the country needs state-driven agrarian development and Filipino industrialization with universal social services.” The government’s solutions to slowing growth and joblessness are ayuda (aka social programs like 4Ps, Tupad, etc.) and the “Big Bold Reforms.” But, as Africa highlighted, the social programs are ineffective against deep poverty because they are low-targeted and patronage-prone. What are the supposed big reforms? Africa described them as “tiny token tweaks that won’t fix the structural problems” because they do not improve the agricultural sector or provide for a progressive taxation system and universal health care. These reforms include 14-day visa-free entry for the Chinese to boost tourism and trade, and ₱4.3-billion support for the auto industry’s Comprehensive Automotive Resurgence Strategy program. Guzman said “the nation’s structure is collapsing” because of political instability and a fragile economy due to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s “blunders.” The first, she said, was adopting an anti-corruption stance in announcing the anomalous flood control projects while remaining silent on the pork barrel issue. She said Marcos Jr.’s disclosure of the flood control projects was intended for him to gain public support. But it failed, she said, for these reasons: First, it enraged the public, especially the poor. Second, it created political fallout with the resignation of officials like Speaker Martin Romualdez and Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co, who chaired the House committee on appropriations. Third, no “big fish” has yet to be formally charged or jailed. The investigation initiated by the President appeared “only to whitewash corruption,” Guzman said, adding that corruption was not accidental or low-level but systemic, needing “approval from the highest level.” Guzman said the President’s second error was “using the 2026 budget to shore up [his] position.” She said the budget still has pork barrel under new names — “allocables,” “unprogrammed appropriations,” “hard” and “soft” pork. As well, she said, confidential and intelligence finds are high and intact, and funding is for debt servicing, not development. Another aspect of the supposed second blunder is framing the 2026 budget as the true education budget, according to Guzman. She declared this a myth because, she said, education is second in priority vis-á-vis infrastructure development. “Education receives a 31-percent increase in allocation while there is a 200-percent increase in construction of educational facilities…” she said. “The education budget is a redistribution of where infrastructure spending can be done.” Guzman described the state of affairs as an example of bureaucrat capitalism marked by, among others, corruption of public funds; turnover of public utilities/assets and natural resources to foreign corporations and local oligarchs; and collusion with criminal syndicates. The political crisis continues, Guzman said, pointing out such identifying factors as intensifying intra-elite rivalry, economic oligarchs’ rule over political parties , and a military “more inclined to constitutional continuity than progressive democratic change.” At the same time, civil society continues to be suppressed, she said, with the administration building up the infrastructure for repression — for example, trumped-up charges against activists — as protests gain momentum over the growing economic distress. Forming part of the crisis is what Guzman termed the “US-subservient, neocolonial foreign policy” of the administration. She cited the Philippines’ military and security alliance with the United States and its serving as a cog in America’s regional defense industrial base. “The US wants the Philippine elite to keep constitutional continuity and avoid sovereignty issues,” she said. Despite the gloomy outlook, Africa and Guzman said the country’s economic and political woes can be ameliorated. Guzman said this can be possible if a plan for industrialization is drawn up. If not, she warned, the country will be trapped in underdevelopment, with a budget that’s pro-elite, anti-poor, and anti-development; an educational system aligned to serve the demand for overseas labor; and repressed freedom. Similarly, Africa raised the urgency of pursuing national industrialization. He admitted to its disruptiveness — “shaking up the status quo, and antagonizing the foreigners who are capitalizing on Filipinos” — but asserted that this long process towards progress has to be done. His slide “Program for National Industrialization” sketched how a democratic, sustainable national industrialization can be drafted into a strategic policy for development. With a broad Filipino industrialization coalition bolstered by patriotism, scientific culture, and a strong mass movement, the policy will prioritize agrarian reform and rural development, advocate protectionism, provide financing for Filipino industrialization, and uplift people’s rights and welfare. Africa declared: “The government shouldn’t be partial to the oligarchs. It must press for the people’s interest rather than the wants of the bureaucrat capitalists.” Receive fresh perspectives and explainers in your inbox every Tuesday and Friday. Since 2016, it has failed to meet its growth targets for the coming year 90 percent of the time.” His data analysis shows that economic growth fell even three years before the pandemic, with the growth for 2025 plunging to a low 5.7 percent. The high growth period of 2004-2016 — 6.6 percent in 2004 and 7.1 percent in 2016 — are long gone, he said, adding: “The economy was growing fast but the slowdown started in 2017 and is continuing up to now, which is contrary to the Marcos Jr. government’s claim of rapid growth.” Africa’s slide presentation titled “Philippine economy after three years of Marcos Jr.” juxtaposed his findings on the growing number of poor and hungry Filipinos vis-á-vis the burgeoning wealth of a few. Figures for the former showed self-rated poor families reaching 14.3 million; involuntary hungry families totaling 5.7 million; and borderline poor and vulnerable families rising to 17.7 million. Conversely, the three richest Filipinos became even richer. According to Africa, Enrique Razon’s wealth increased 115 percent or an additional ₱351 billion; Ramon Ang’s wealth rose by 62 percent or an additional ₱83 billion; and Manny Villar’s wealth grew by 48 percent or an additional ₱203 billion. Africa said household spending was the biggest driver for economic growth because of the “additional 10 million [people] spending.” But household spending weakened after 2017, when wage increase stagnated, remittances from overseas dropped, and foreign direct investment inflows fell. Services filled the gap but they were not of high quality and could not compensate for the lost jobs in the agriculture and manufacturing sectors, he said. He argued that external sources should not be driving growth, and pointed out that “the country needs state-driven agrarian development and Filipino industrialization with universal social services.” The government’s solutions to slowing growth and joblessness are ayuda (aka social programs like 4Ps, Tupad, etc.) and the “Big Bold Reforms.” But, as Africa highlighted, the social programs are ineffective against deep poverty because they are low-targeted and patronage-prone. What are the supposed big reforms? Africa described them as “tiny token tweaks that won’t fix the structural problems” because they do not improve the agricultural sector or provide for a progressive taxation system and universal health care. These reforms include 14-day visa-free entry for the Chinese to boost tourism and trade, and ₱4.3-billion support for the auto industry’s Comprehensive Automotive Resurgence Strategy program. Guzman said “the nation’s structure is collapsing” because of political instability and a fragile economy due to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s “blunders.” The first, she said, was adopting an anti-corruption stance in announcing the anomalous flood control projects while remaining silent on the pork barrel issue. She said Marcos Jr.’s disclosure of the flood control projects was intended for him to gain public support. But it failed, she said, for these reasons: First, it enraged the public, especially the poor. Second, it created political fallout with the resignation of officials like Speaker Martin Romualdez and Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co, who chaired the House committee on appropriations. Third, no “big fish” has yet to be formally charged or jailed. The investigation initiated by the President appeared “only to whitewash corruption,” Guzman said, adding that corruption was not accidental or low-level but systemic, needing “approval from the highest level.” Guzman said the President’s second error was “using the 2026 budget to shore up [his] position.” She said the budget still has pork barrel under new names — “allocables,” “unprogrammed appropriations,” “hard” and “soft” pork. As well, she said, confidential and intelligence finds are high and intact, and funding is for debt servicing, not development. Another aspect of the supposed second blunder is framing the 2026 budget as the true education budget, according to Guzman. She declared this a myth because, she said, education is second in priority vis-á-vis infrastructure development. “Education receives a 31-percent increase in allocation while there is a 200-percent increase in construction of educational facilities…” she said. “The education budget is a redistribution of where infrastructure spending can be done.” Guzman described the state of affairs as an example of bureaucrat capitalism marked by, among others, corruption of public funds; turnover of public utilities/assets and natural resources to foreign corporations and local oligarchs; and collusion with criminal syndicates. The political crisis continues, Guzman said, pointing out such identifying factors as intensifying intra-elite rivalry, economic oligarchs’ rule over political parties , and a military “more inclined to constitutional continuity than progressive democratic change.” At the same time, civil society continues to be suppressed, she said, with the administration building up the infrastructure for repression — for example, trumped-up charges against activists — as protests gain momentum over the growing economic distress. Forming part of the crisis is what Guzman termed the “US-subservient, neocolonial foreign policy” of the administration. She cited the Philippines’ military and security alliance with the United States and its serving as a cog in America’s regional defense industrial base. “The US wants the Philippine elite to keep constitutional continuity and avoid sovereignty issues,” she said. Despite the gloomy outlook, Africa and Guzman said the country’s economic and political woes can be ameliorated. Guzman said this can be possible if a plan for industrialization is drawn up. If not, she warned, the country will be trapped in underdevelopment, with a budget that’s pro-elite, anti-poor, and anti-development; an educational system aligned to serve the demand for overseas labor; and repressed freedom. Similarly, Africa raised the urgency of pursuing national industrialization. He admitted to its disruptiveness — “shaking up the status quo, and antagonizing the foreigners who are capitalizing on Filipinos” — but asserted that this long process towards progress has to be done. His slide “Program for National Industrialization” sketched how a democratic, sustainable national industrialization can be drafted into a strategic policy for development. With a broad Filipino industrialization coalition bolstered by patriotism, scientific culture, and a strong mass movement, the policy will prioritize agrarian reform and rural development, advocate protectionism, provide financing for Filipino industrialization, and uplift people’s rights and welfare. Africa declared: “The government shouldn’t be partial to the oligarchs. output.text: Two Facebook (FB) users published a misleading graphic showing different infrastructure projects that supposedly serve as the “legacy” of previous administrations. The posts dated Feb. 9 and 19 showed three bridges. It credited the following to two “corrupt” presidents: It then attributed to a “not corrupt” president, the late Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III, a wooden bridge in Zamboanga City that caved in. It is a fact that the San Juanico Bridge, which connects Samar and Leyte, was built during Marcos’ term. And it is also true that the collapsed wooden footbridge was part of the Aquino administration’s Zamboanga City Roadmap to Recovery and Reconstruction Program , according to a 2018 FB post of Zamboanga City Mayor Beng Climaco. However, the CCLEX is a project that commenced not under Duterte but Aquino, who was president from June 2010 to June 2016. Studies for the construction of the bridge were conducted in 2014 . In January 2016, the Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MTPC) filed a disclosure form stating it received notices of award for “the financing, design, construction, implementation, operation and maintenance” of the bridge. (Read related story: VERA FILES FACT CHECK: Crediting Mark Villar, Duterte’s ‘Build, Build, Build’ for Cebu bridge started during Aquino’s term needs context ) The CCLEX is a joint venture project signed in April 2016 between the MTPC in collaboration with the City of Cebu and the municipality of Cordova. The 8.9-kilometer expressway will be the longest bridge in the country once construction is completed. A netizen, criticizing one of the posts, said the CCLEX is a Public-Private Partnership project and that credit should instead go to the local government units involved.
